# Brindle Cheese Cellar Handbook

## Ripening rooms

The Brindle cellar's wash-rind cheeses are turned and washed every other day for the first three weeks, using a brine of 6 percent salt that is made fresh on the Monday and thrown out on the Friday. The washing cloth is boiled between rooms, and the person who washes the young cheeses never washes the blue ones in the same shift, because the blue mould spreads on the cloth and settles on the rinds where it is not wanted and cannot be removed without scraping the cheese to the paste.

Humidity in the first ripening room is held at 92 percent and the temperature at 12 degrees, and both are read from the wall hygrometer at opening and closing time. The cellar master writes the readings on the board by the door, and a reading outside the range is reported on the spot rather than at the end of the week, since a room that has drifted for a few days has already spoiled a batch and nothing can be done about it later.

The oldest vats in the cellar are the stone ones at the north end, and they are scrubbed with a stiff brush and plain hot water, never with soap or bleach. The scrubbing is done on the first Tuesday of the month, and the vats are left to air for two full days before any milk is brought near them, because a trace of cleaner in the stone is carried into the curd and gives a flat, soapy taste to the whole batch.

Cheeses that are ready are tasted by two people, and are released for sale only when both agree. A wheel is sold when it has ripened for at least 63 days and the rind has formed a firm, dry skin without cracks. The tasting notes are kept in the green ledger, and a wheel that fails twice is cut up for the kitchen and recorded as a loss, not quietly sold at a discount to a customer who trusts the label.
